````math
## Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO

### F.1 The Critique-GRPO Algorithm

The Critique-GRPO algorithm is summarized in
Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ F.1 The Critique-GRPO Algorithm ‣ Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").

1:  Input: Pretrained policy $`\pi_{\text{old}}`$ ($`\theta`$), reward
model $`\pi_{RM}`$, questions $`Q`$, instructions
$`I_{\text{refine}},I_{c}`$

2:  Goal: Improve policy by learning from initial responses and
critiques

3:  // Step 1: Initial Response Sampling

4:  for each question $`q\in Q`$ do

5:   Sample $`n`$ initial responses:
$`\{y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n}\sim\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot|q)`$

6:   Generate CoT critiques:
$`\{c_{\text{CoT}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n}\sim\pi_{RM}(\cdot\mid I_{c},q,y^{(i)})`$

7:   Obtain scalar rewards: $`\{R^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$ from $`\pi_{RM}`$
labels

8:  end for

9:  // Step 2: Critique-Guided Self-Refinement

10:  for each response $`y^{(i)}\in\{y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$ do

11:   Generate refinement:
$`y_{\text{refined}}^{(i)}\sim\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot\mid I_{\text{refine}},q,y^{(i)},c_{\text{CoT}}^{(i)})`$

12:   Score refinement:
$`R_{\text{refine}}^{(i)}\leftarrow\text{Eval}(y_{\text{refined}}^{(i)})`$

13:  end for

14:  Sample $`k`$ refinements to mitigate shift:
$`\{y_{\text{refined}}^{(i^{\prime})}\}_{i^{\prime}=1}^{k}\subset\{y_{\text{refined}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$

15:  Form mixed group:
$`\mathcal{Y}_{\text{mix}}=\{y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n}\cup\{y_{\text{refined}}^{(i^{\prime})}\}_{i^{\prime}=1}^{k}`$

16:  // Step 3: Online Policy Optimization

17:  Compute token-level advantage $`\hat{A}_{t}`$ for
$`\mathcal{Y}_{\text{mix}}`$ using group relative rewards

18:  Calculate ratios $`r_{t}(\theta)`$ and apply policy shaping for
refinements $`r_{\text{refine},t}(\theta)`$

19:  Update $`\theta`$ by maximizing
$`\mathcal{J}_{\text{Critique-GRPO}}`$
(Eq. [2](#S4.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 4.2 Online RL with Critique-GRPO ‣ 4 Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"))

20:  Output: Fine-tuned policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$

Algorithm 2 Critique-GRPO: Online Policy Optimization Framework

### F.2 The shaping Function in Critique-GRPO

![Refer to
caption](2506.03106v7/floats/raw_figures/function_plot_with_gamma.png)

Figure 8: Effect of $`\gamma`$ on the shaping function $`f(x)`$. The
black dashed diagonal line indicates no shaping, $`f(x)=x`$.

We adopt a shaping function $`f(x)=x/(x+\gamma)`$([Yan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib42)) ($`0<\gamma<1`$), depicted in
Figure[8](#A6.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ F.2 The shaping Function in Critique-GRPO ‣ Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
to reweight gradients and emphasize low-probability tokens in refined
responses. As illustrated in
Figure [8](#A6.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ F.2 The shaping Function in Critique-GRPO ‣ Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
this function is bounded between $`(0,1)`$, where $`x`$ represents the
token probability of the policy. When $`\gamma`$ is small (*i.e.,* 0.1),
the function significantly amplifies low probabilities, with this
amplification decreasing as $`x`$ increases. Larger $`\gamma`$ values
(0.9) produce less pronounced scaling effects. The black dashed diagonal
line indicates no shaping (*i.e.,* $`f(x)=x`$). We set $`\gamma=0.1`$ to
optimize learning from unfamiliar yet correct refinements while strongly
penalizing unfamiliar incorrect ones.

### F.3 Ratio of Responses per Prompt in Critique-GRPO

We experiment with the ratio of initial responses to refinements per
prompt, ranging from 1:1 to 7:1. Our results indicate that a 7:1 ratio
achieves both stable training and optimal performance. Lower ratios lead
to performance degradation due to sudden increases in entropy loss,
caused by distribution shifts introduced by the refinements, during
later training stages.

### F.4 Theoretical Analysis of Sample Efficiency

In this section, we provide a theoretical justification for the superior
sample efficiency of critique-guided refinement compared to standard
reward-based learning. We utilize the Transfer Eluder Dimension ([Xu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib25)) framework to quantify the information gain
provided by language feedback. We first formalize our critique mechanism
as Reward-Informative Feedback, establishing that it allows the policy
to distinguish hypotheses significantly more efficiently than scalar
rewards alone. We then apply this framework to reasoning tasks to
demonstrate an exponential reduction in sample complexity.

##### Preliminaries: Complexity Measures and Verifiers.

To characterize the complexity of the hypothesis space $`\mathcal{H}`$,
we first introduce the Eluder Dimension ([Russo and Van Roy,
2013](#bib.bib23)), a standard measure in reinforcement learning that
quantifies how many observations are required to reduce uncertainty
about a reward function.

###### Definition F.1 (Eluder Dimension ([Russo and Van Roy, 2013](#bib.bib23))).

An action $`a\in\mathcal{A}`$ is $`\epsilon`$-dependent on actions
$`\{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\}\subset\mathcal{A}`$ with respect to a reward
class $`\mathcal{R}`$ if any pair of reward functions
$`r,r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}`$ satisfying
$`\sum_{i=1}^{n}(r(a_{i})-r^{\prime}(a_{i}))^{2}\leq\epsilon^{2}`$ also
satisfies $`|r(a)-r^{\prime}(a)|\leq\epsilon`$. The $`\epsilon`$-eluder
dimension, denoted $`\dim_{E}(\mathcal{R},\epsilon)`$, is the length of
the longest sequence in $`\mathcal{A}`$ such that every element is
$`\epsilon^{\prime}`$-independent of its predecessors for some
$`\epsilon^{\prime}\geq\epsilon`$.

In Language Learning from Feedback (LLF) ([Cheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib8)), agents leverage feedback $`o`$ (*e.g.,* critiques)
beyond scalar rewards. To quantify the information in $`o`$, we assume
the existence of a verifier.

###### Assumption F.2 (Verifier ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib25))).

The verifier defines a loss
$`\ell:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{H}\to[0,1]`$ measuring
the alignment between a hypothesis $`\eta`$ and feedback $`o`$ on action
$`a`$. Consistency yields $`\ell(a,o,\eta)=0`$, while inconsistency
incurs a non-zero penalty.

To accommodate potential noise, we assume feedback is unbiased: each
hypothesis minimizes the expected verifier loss under its induced
distribution. Defining the expected minimum loss as
$`\ell^{\min}_{\eta}(a):=\min_{\eta^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}_{o\sim f_{\eta}(a)}[\ell(a,o,\eta^{\prime})]`$,
we utilize this to define the Transfer Eluder Dimension:

###### Definition F.3 (Transfer Eluder Dimension ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib25))).

An action $`a`$ is $`\epsilon`$-transfer dependent on actions
$`\{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\}\subset\mathcal{A}`$ with respect to
$`\mathcal{H}`$ and verifier $`\ell`$ if any pair
$`\eta,\eta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}`$ satisfying:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathbb{E}_{o\sim f_{\eta^{\prime}}(a_{i})}[\ell(a_{i},o,\eta)]-\ell^{\min}_{\eta^{\prime}}(a_{i})\right)\leq\epsilon^{2}
``` |  | (7) |

also satisfies $`|r_{\eta}(a)-r_{\eta^{\prime}}(a)|\leq\epsilon`$. The
$`\epsilon`$-transfer eluder dimension,
$`\dim_{TE}(\mathcal{H},\ell,\epsilon)`$, is the length of the longest
sequence of transfer-independent actions.

##### Critique as Reward-Informative Feedback.

Intuitively, the Transfer Eluder Dimension measures how effectively
feedback reduces uncertainty about the reward. For this framework to
apply, we must establish that our critique mechanism is at least as
useful as the reward signal. We rely on the concept of
Reward-Informative Feedback.

###### Definition F.4 (Reward-Informative Feedback).

A feedback function $`f_{\eta}`$ is reward-informative of $`r_{\eta}`$
with respect to a verifier $`\ell`$ if there exists a constant
$`C_{F}>0`$ such that for all $`\eta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}`$ and
$`a\in\mathcal{A}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
|r_{\eta}(a)-r_{\eta^{\prime}}(a)|^{2}\leq C_{F}\mathbb{E}_{o\sim f_{\eta}(a)}[\ell(a,o,\eta^{\prime})-\ell^{\min}_{\eta}(a)].
``` |  | (8) |

This condition implies that if two hypotheses differ in reward, the
verifier can distinguish them via feedback. Our employed critiques (both
indicative and constructive) satisfy this condition by providing
strictly more information than a binary reward $`r\in\{0,1\}`$, enabling
the rejection of incorrect hypotheses without needing to observe the
final scalar reward.

###### Proposition F.5 (Generalization Bound).

For reward-informative LLF problems with constant $`C_{F}`$, the
Transfer Eluder Dimension is bounded by the standard Eluder Dimension of
the effective reward class
$`\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{H}}=\{r_{\eta}:\eta\in\mathcal{H}\}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\dim_{TE}(\mathcal{H},C_{F}\ell,\epsilon)\leq\dim_{E}(\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{H}},\epsilon).
``` |  | (9) |

Proposition
[F.5](#A6.Thmtheorem5 "Proposition F.5 (Generalization Bound). ‣ Critique as Reward-Informative Feedback. ‣ F.4 Theoretical Analysis of Sample Efficiency ‣ Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")
guarantees that learning from critiques is no harder than learning from
rewards. However, in practice, the inequality is strict and the gap is
large. Below, we quantify this gap for reasoning tasks.

##### Complexity Reduction Analysis.

We analyze the reduction in the effective search space for a reasoning
task where the goal is to construct a hidden optimal solution sequence
$`a^{*}=(s^{*}_{1},\dots,s^{*}_{L})`$ of length $`L`$ over a vocabulary
$`\mathcal{S}`$. The action space is defined as
$`\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{S}^{L}`$.

###### Proposition F.6 (Sample Efficiency of Critique-Guided Refinement).

We compare the dimension of the hypothesis space under Reward-Only
Learning versus Critique-Guided Learning.

1.  1.
    Standard Generation – Reward-Only Learning (Eluder Dimension): With
    binary rewards $`r(a)=\mathbb{I}(a=a^{*})`$, the signal is sparse (a
    “needle in a haystack”). Observing $`r(a)=0`$ eliminates only the
    specific sequence $`a`$, providing no information about the
    correctness of other sequences $`a^{\prime}\neq a`$. Consequently,
    the agent must effectively enumerate the action space to find
    $`a^{*}`$. The Eluder dimension scales exponentially with the
    sequence length:

    |     |                                                             |     |      |
    |-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \dim_{E}(\mathcal{R},\epsilon)\approx O(|\mathcal{S}|^{L}).
           ```                                                          |     | (10) |
2.  2.
    Critique-Guided Refinement – Critique-Guided Learning (Transfer
    Eluder Dimension): We analyze two types of feedback mechanisms:

    - •
      Indicative Feedback ($`c_{\text{I}}`$, $`c_{\text{GT}}`$): This
      feedback indicates failure but lacks specific error localization.
      While the worst-case complexity remains
      $`\dim_{TE}(\mathcal{H},\ell,\epsilon)\approx O(|\mathcal{S}|^{L})`$,
      the critique acts as a pruning signal. Conditioning on the failure
      and the specific content of the critique restricts the search to a
      subspace $`\mathcal{A}_{c}\subset\mathcal{A}`$, reducing the
      effective search space size by a constant factor $`\alpha<1`$.
    - •
      Constructive Feedback ($`c_{\text{CoT}}`$): If the critique
      localizes the first error at step $`t`$, the problem decomposes
      into $`L`$ sequential sub-problems, each of size
      $`|\mathcal{S}|`$. This reduces the complexity from exponential to
      linear, *i.e.,*
      $`\dim_{TE}(\mathcal{H},\ell,\epsilon)\approx O(L|\mathcal{S}|)`$.
      Furthermore, if the critique provides the correction suggestion
      for the first error $`s_{t}^{*}`$, the complexity becomes
      independent of the vocabulary size, scaling as
      $`\dim_{TE}(\mathcal{H},\ell,\epsilon)\approx O(L)`$.

Consequently, for a fixed computational budget $`M`$ where
$`L|\mathcal{S}|\ll M\ll|\mathcal{S}|^{L}`$, critique-guided exploration
yields a significantly higher probability of success:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P(a^{*}\in\{y_{\text{refined}}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{M})\gg P(a^{*}\in\{y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{M}).
``` |  | (11) |

###### Proof.

We prove this by estimating the Transfer Eluder Dimension $`d`$, which
quantifies the effective search space size. We assume a uniform
exploration strategy over the effective search space.

1. Derivation of Effective Dimension ($`d`$)

Case A: Reward-Only. The binary indicator problem is equivalent to a
standard bandit problem with $`|\mathcal{S}|^{L}`$ arms. In this
setting, the feedback function is simply the reward itself,
$`f_{\eta}(a)=r(a)`$. Observing $`r(a)=0`$ provides information only
about action $`a`$ and no other $`a^{\prime}\neq a`$. Thus,
$`a^{\prime}`$ is $`\epsilon`$-independent of $`a`$ (Definition
[F.1](#A6.Thmtheorem1 "Definition F.1 (Eluder Dimension ( , )). ‣ Preliminaries: Complexity Measures and Verifiers. ‣ F.4 Theoretical Analysis of Sample Efficiency ‣ Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")).
We can construct a sequence of independent actions spanning the entire
space. Thus, the dimension is bounded by the cardinality of the action
space:

|     |                                   |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       d_{\text{std}}=|\mathcal{S}|^{L}.
       ```                                |     | (12) |

Case B: Critique-Guided (Constructive). Let the feedback $`f(a)`$ return
the index of the first error: $`t=\min\{i\mid s_{i}\neq s^{*}_{i}\}`$.
We partition the action space $`\mathcal{A}`$ into $`L`$ disjoint sets,
where
$`\mathcal{A}_{t}=\{(s_{1},\dots,s_{L})\mid s_{1:t-1}\text{ are correct, }s_{t}\text{ is incorrect}\}`$.
According to Definition
[F.3](#A6.Thmtheorem3 "Definition F.3 (Transfer Eluder Dimension ( , )). ‣ Preliminaries: Complexity Measures and Verifiers. ‣ F.4 Theoretical Analysis of Sample Efficiency ‣ Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
an action is transfer-dependent if similar feedback implies similar
rewards. If we select more than $`|\mathcal{S}|`$ actions from a
partition $`\mathcal{A}_{t}`$, by the Pigeonhole Principle, at least two
actions must share the same incorrect token $`s_{t}`$ (given they share
the same correct prefix). Observing the error index $`t`$ for the first
action effectively predicts the error index for the second. This reduces
the problem to solving $`L`$ sequential classification problems of size
$`|\mathcal{S}|`$. The effective dimension is the sum of these
sub-problems:

|     |                                                             |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       d_{\text{crit}}=\sum_{t=1}^{L}|\mathcal{S}|=L|\mathcal{S}|.
       ```                                                          |     | (13) |

If the critique also provides the correction suggestion for the first
error $`s_{t}^{*}`$, the sequence of error indices in an independent
action sequence becomes strictly monotonic, further reducing the
dimension to $`d_{\text{corr}}\approx O(L)`$.

2. Probability of Success

Let $`M`$ be the computational budget. The probability of finding the
unique optimal solution $`a^{*}`$ is equivalent to sampling the correct
element from a set of size $`d`$ without replacement. The probability of
success is approximately:

|     |                                                           |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       P(\text{success})\approx 1-\exp\left(-\frac{M}{d}\right).
       ```                                                        |     | (14) |

Given the regime $`L|\mathcal{S}|\ll M\ll|\mathcal{S}|^{L}`$:

For Reward-Only Learning, substituting
$`d_{\text{std}}=|\mathcal{S}|^{L}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P_{\text{std}}\approx 1-\exp\left(-\frac{M}{|\mathcal{S}|^{L}}\right)\approx\frac{M}{|\mathcal{S}|^{L}}\approx 0.
``` |  | (15) |

For Critique-Guided Learning, substituting
$`d_{\text{crit}}=L|\mathcal{S}|`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P_{\text{crit}}\approx 1-\exp\left(-\frac{M}{L|\mathcal{S}|}\right)\approx 1.
``` |  | (16) |

Conclusion. The ratio of success probabilities is
$`\frac{P_{\text{crit}}}{P_{\text{std}}}\approx\frac{|\mathcal{S}|^{L}}{M}\gg 1`$.
This confirms that critique-guided refinement is strictly more
sample-efficient than standard reward-based generation. ∎

### F.5 Theoretical Analysis of Convergence and Policy Improvement

Building upon the sample efficiency established in
Appendix [F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 Theoretical Analysis of Sample Efficiency ‣ Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
we now analyze the optimization dynamics. We prove that while standard
GRPO converges given sufficient samples, Critique-GRPO accelerates this
process by altering the trajectory distribution. We utilize the
framework of Policy Gradient methods ([Sutton et al., 1999](#bib.bib2);
[Agarwal et al., 2021](#bib.bib3)) to demonstrate that Critique-GRPO
learns from higher quality trajectories, guaranteeing a steeper
monotonic policy improvement.

##### Preliminaries and Problem Setup.

We consider the reasoning task as a contextual bandit problem ([Lu et
al., 2010](#bib.bib10)). Let $`\pi_{\theta}(y|x)`$ be the policy
parameterized by $`\theta`$.

###### Definition F.7 (Sparse Reward Landscape).

The reward function $`R(y,x)`$ is binary and sparse. Let
$`\mathcal{Y}^{*}_{x}`$ be the set of correct reasoning chains.

|     |                                             |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(y,x)=\mathbb{I}(y\in\mathcal{Y}^{*}_{x}).
       ```                                          |     | (17) |

###### Definition F.8 (GRPO Gradient Estimate).

Following [Shao et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib5), GRPO estimates the gradient
using a group of $`G`$ outputs $`\{y_{1},\dots,y_{G}\}`$ sampled from
$`\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}`$ for a single input $`x`$. The gradient
estimator is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{g}_{\text{GRPO}}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\hat{A}_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x),\quad\text{where }\hat{A}_{i}=\frac{R(y_{i})-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}+\epsilon}.
``` |  | (18) |

#### F.5.1 Inefficiency of Standard Exploration

In complex reasoning tasks, the probability of generating a correct
solution $`y^{*}`$ via random sampling, denoted as
$`p^{*}=P_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}}(y\in\mathcal{Y}^{*}_{x})`$, is small but
non-negligible. While standard GRPO is an unbiased estimator, its
convergence rate is limited by the sparsity of the signal.

###### Proposition F.9 (Signal-to-Noise Ratio in Standard GRPO).

For a group size $`G`$, the expected number of positive rewards in a
standard GRPO batch is $`\mathbb{E}[N^{+}]=Gp^{*}`$. The gradient
contribution from optimal trajectories is weighted by $`p^{*}`$. If
$`p^{*}<1/G`$, many batches will contain no positive signal
($`\sigma_{R}=0`$), resulting in wasted computation steps where
$`\Delta\theta=0`$. Even when $`\sigma_{R}>0`$, the magnitude of the
update in the direction of the optimal policy is proportional to
$`p^{*}`$.

#### F.5.2 Policy Improvement via Critique-Guided Refinement

Critique-GRPO modifies the sampling distribution. Instead of optimizing
solely on $`y\sim\pi_{\theta}`$, we optimize on a mixture distribution
induced by the critique mechanism. Let the refined set be
$`\mathcal{Y}_{\text{ref}}=\{\text{Refine}(y)\mid y\sim\pi_{\theta}\}`$.

###### Lemma F.10 (Trajectory Quality Enhancement).

Let $`P_{\text{crit}}`$ be the success rate of the critique mechanism in
generating a correct solution $`y^{*}`$. As shown in
Proposition [4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition 4.1 (Complexity Reduction via Critique-Guided Exploration). ‣ 4.2 Online RL with Critique-GRPO ‣ 4 Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
$`P_{\text{crit}}\gg p^{*}`$. By including $`\mathcal{Y}_{\text{ref}}`$
in the GRPO group, the effective probability of observing an optimal
trajectory in the batch becomes
$`P_{\text{eff}}\approx P_{\text{crit}}`$. This ensures that the
gradient estimator is dominated by high-quality trajectories,
significantly reducing the variance of the advantage function and
ensuring $`\sigma_{R}>0`$ with high probability.

We now prove that learning from these higher-quality trajectories leads
to superior policy improvement.

###### Theorem F.11 (Policy Improvement Lower Bound).

Let $`\pi_{\text{old}}`$ be the current policy and $`\pi_{\text{new}}`$
be the policy after an update step with learning rate $`\alpha`$. The
expected improvement in the objective function $`J(\pi)`$ is
lower-bounded by the quality of the trajectories used in the update.
Comparing Standard GRPO and Critique-GRPO:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta J_{\text{std}}`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq\alpha\cdot p^{*}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\sigma_{R}}\pi_{\text{old}}(y^{*})\|\nabla\log\pi(y^{*})\|^{2}\right]-O(\alpha^{2})`$ |  | (19) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta J_{\text{crit}}`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq\alpha\cdot P_{\text{crit}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\sigma_{R}}\pi_{\text{old}}(y^{*})\|\nabla\log\pi(y^{*})\|^{2}\right]-O(\alpha^{2})`$ |  | (20) |

Since $`P_{\text{crit}}\gg p^{*}`$, it follows that
$`\Delta J_{\text{crit}}\gg\Delta J_{\text{std}}`$.

###### Proof.

Step 1: Performance Difference. From [Kakade and Langford
(2002)](#bib.bib11),
$`J(\pi_{\text{new}})-J(\pi_{\text{old}})\approx\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\rho}[\hat{A}(y)]`$,
where $`\rho`$ is the sampling distribution. The update vector
$`\Delta\theta`$ is proportional to the advantage-weighted gradient:
$`\Delta\theta\propto\sum_{y\in\text{Batch}}\hat{A}(y)\nabla\log\pi(y)`$.

Step 2: Dominance of Optimal Trajectories. In a sparse reward setting,
the advantage of an optimal solution $`y^{*}`$ is positive and large,
while incorrect solutions have small negative advantages. The update
direction is dominated by the term corresponding to $`y^{*}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta\theta\approx\eta\cdot\hat{A}(y^{*})\nabla\log\pi(y^{*}).
``` |  | (21) |

The magnitude of this update depends on the frequency of observing
$`y^{*}`$ in the batch.

Step 3: Comparison of Sampling Distributions.

- •
  Standard GRPO: Samples $`y\sim\pi_{\text{old}}`$. The probability of
  observing $`y^{*}`$ is $`p^{*}`$. The expected update norm is
  proportional to $`p^{*}\|\nabla\log\pi(y^{*})\|`$.
- •
  Critique-GRPO: Samples from a mixture including refined outputs. The
  probability of observing $`y^{*}`$ is $`P_{\text{crit}}`$. The
  expected update norm is proportional to
  $`P_{\text{crit}}\|\nabla\log\pi(y^{*})\|`$.

Conclusion: The superiority of Critique-GRPO lies in the fact that it
learns from a distribution of higher trajectories. Even if standard
exploration is capable of finding the solution (non-negligible
$`p^{*}`$), the critique mechanism artificially amplifies the density of
optimal solutions in the training data. Substituting the observation
probabilities into the Taylor expansion of the objective function:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J(\pi_{\text{new}})-J(\pi_{\text{old}})\approx\nabla J(\pi_{\text{old}})^{\top}\Delta\theta\propto P(\text{observing }y^{*})\cdot\|\nabla\log\pi(y^{*})\|^{2}.
``` |  | (22) |

Given $`P_{\text{crit}}\gg p^{*}`$, the lower bound on policy
improvement is strictly higher for Critique-GRPO. ∎

###### Theorem F.12 (Global Convergence via Policy Shaping).

Assuming the function approximation class of $`\pi_{\theta}`$ is
sufficiently expressive and the learning rate satisfies Robbins-Monro
conditions, Critique-GRPO converges to the optimal policy $`\pi^{*}`$.
The convergence rate is accelerated by a factor of
$`O(P_{\text{crit}}/p^{*})`$ compared to standard GRPO.

###### Proof.

We utilize the property that Critique-GRPO simulates Supervised
Fine-Tuning (SFT) on dynamically generated optimal data within the RL
loop. From
Theorem [F.11](#A6.Thmtheorem11 "Theorem F.11 (Policy Improvement Lower Bound). ‣ F.5.2 Policy Improvement via Critique-Guided Refinement ‣ F.5 Theoretical Analysis of Convergence and Policy Improvement ‣ Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
the policy probability mass on $`y^{*}`$ increases at each step. Since
the gradient variance is bounded (due to the high probability of
non-zero variance batches via
Lemma [F.10](#A6.Thmtheorem10 "Lemma F.10 (Trajectory Quality Enhancement). ‣ F.5.2 Policy Improvement via Critique-Guided Refinement ‣ F.5 Theoretical Analysis of Convergence and Policy Improvement ‣ Appendix F More Details about Critique-GRPO ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")),
stochastic gradient descent converges. Crucially, the effective learning
rate on the optimal trajectory $`y^{*}`$ is scaled by the critique
success rate. Thus, the model requires fewer iterations to reach the
same level of performance as standard GRPO, effectively leveraging the
higher quality of the critique-refined trajectories. ∎

### F.6 Theoretical Analysis: Gradient Efficiency and Manifold Preservation

Now we provide a analysis of the optimization dynamics in
$`\mathcal{J}_{\text{Critique-GRPO}}`$ after employing the shaping
function on the refinements. We address the dual challenge of (1)
efficiently extracting learning signals from off-policy refined
responses ($`y_{\text{ref}}`$) and (2) preventing the catastrophic
forgetting (entropy explosion) caused by distribution shift.

#### F.6.1 Gradient Dynamics of the Shaping Function

Standard Policy Gradient methods maximize
$`\mathbb{E}[\log\pi_{\theta}(y)]`$. However, for refined responses
where $`\pi_{\theta}(y_{\text{ref}})\ll 1`$, standard gradients can be
unstable or vanish. We employ the shaping function
$`\rho_{t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{t}}{\pi_{t}+\gamma}`$.

###### Lemma F.13 (Gradient Rescaling).

Let $`\pi_{t}=\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})`$. The gradient of the shaped
objective with respect to the policy parameters $`\theta`$ is a
re-weighted version of the standard policy gradient:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla_{\theta}\rho_{t}(\theta)=\underbrace{\left[\frac{\gamma\pi_{t}}{(\pi_{t}+\gamma)^{2}}\right]}_{\Psi(\pi_{t})}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{t}.
``` |  | (23) |

###### Proof.

Applying the quotient rule to $`\rho_{t}`$ with respect to $`\pi_{t}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\partial\rho_{t}}{\partial\pi_{t}}=\frac{1\cdot(\pi_{t}+\gamma)-\pi_{t}\cdot 1}{(\pi_{t}+\gamma)^{2}}=\frac{\gamma}{(\pi_{t}+\gamma)^{2}}.
``` |  | (24) |

By the chain rule,
$`\nabla_{\theta}\rho_{t}=\frac{\partial\rho_{t}}{\partial\pi_{t}}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{t}`$.
Using the log-derivative identity
$`\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{t}=\pi_{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{t}`$, we
substitute to obtain:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla_{\theta}\rho_{t}=\frac{\gamma\pi_{t}}{(\pi_{t}+\gamma)^{2}}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{t}.
``` |  | (25) |

∎

##### Analysis of the Modulation Term $`\Psi(\pi_{t})`$.

The coefficient $`\Psi(\pi_{t})`$ acts as a dynamic gain controller,
theoretically aligning with the ”hard negative mining” mechanism found
in Focal Loss ([Lin et al., 2017](#bib.bib9)).

1.  1.
    Suppression of Easy Tokens ($`\pi_{t}\to 1`$):
    $`\lim_{\pi_{t}\to 1}\Psi(\pi_{t})\approx\frac{\gamma}{(1+\gamma)^{2}}`$.
    Since $`\gamma\ll 1`$, the gradient magnitude is significantly
    dampened. This prevents the model from overfitting to tokens it has
    already mastered, preserving the KL-divergence on trivial tokens.
2.  2.
    Peak Efficiency in the Learning Zone: Solving
    $`\frac{d\Psi}{d\pi}=0`$ yields a maximum at $`\pi_{t}=\gamma`$. By
    setting $`\gamma\approx 0.1`$, we explicitly maximize gradients for
    ”correction tokens”—those that the current policy considers unlikely
    but plausible. This focuses the update on the reasoning gap between
    the initial and refined response.

#### F.6.2 The Insufficiency of Clipping for Off-Policy Data

Standard PPO/GRPO relies on clipping the probability ratio $`r_{t}`$ to
$`[1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]`$ to enforce a trust region ([Schulman et al.,
2017](#bib.bib43)). While effective for on-policy data, we prove that
clipping is insufficient for off-policy refinements due to vector
orthogonality.

###### Proposition F.14 (Gradient Orthogonality).

Let $`\mathcal{M}_{\text{old}}`$ be the manifold of the current policy.
The gradient update from refinements, $`\Delta\theta_{\text{ref}}`$, is
often orthogonal to the update from initial responses,
$`\Delta\theta_{\text{init}}`$.

Reasoning: $`\Delta\theta_{\text{init}}`$ reinforces the current mode of
the distribution. Conversely, $`\Delta\theta_{\text{ref}}`$ attempts to
shift probability mass to a disjoint region of the sample space
($`y_{\text{ref}}`$). Optimizing $`\Delta\theta_{\text{ref}}`$
inherently requires reducing the probability of $`y_{\text{init}}`$.
Therefore:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\langle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J}_{\text{init}},\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J}_{\text{ref}}\rangle<0.
``` |  | (26) |

Clipping bounds the magnitude of the step but does not correct this
conflicting direction. Without regularization, the accumulation of
$`\Delta\theta_{\text{ref}}`$ updates drags the policy off the manifold
$`\mathcal{M}_{\text{old}}`$, leading to entropy collapse.

#### F.6.3 Manifold Preservation via The Anchor Hypothesis

To prevent this collapse, we derive the necessity of the sample
prioritization ratio $`N_{\text{init}}\gg N_{\text{ref}}`$.

###### Theorem F.15 (The Anchor Condition).

Let $`\mathbf{F}`$ be the Fisher Information Matrix of the policy. To
ensure the updated policy $`\pi_{\theta^{\prime}}`$ remains within a
trust region
$`D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta^{\prime}}||\pi_{\theta})\leq\delta`$, the
influence of refined samples must be bounded by the curvature of the
on-policy manifold.

###### Proof.

We approximate the KL divergence using the second-order Taylor expansion
([Amari et al., 2019](#bib.bib7); [Kakade and Langford,
2002](#bib.bib11)):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta+\Delta\theta}||\pi_{\theta})\approx\frac{1}{2}\Delta\theta^{T}\mathbf{F}\Delta\theta.
``` |  | (27) |

The total update is a convex combination:
$`\Delta\theta\propto(1-\lambda)g_{\text{init}}+\lambda g_{\text{ref}}`$,
where $`\lambda=N_{\text{ref}}/N`$. Since $`g_{\text{init}}`$ is clipped
on-policy, its contribution to the divergence is bounded by design. The
risk arises from $`g_{\text{ref}}`$, which is high-variance and
off-distribution. If $`\lambda`$ is large, the term
$`\lambda g_{\text{ref}}`$ dominates. Since $`g_{\text{ref}}`$ is not
aligned with the eigenvectors of $`\mathbf{F}`$ (which represent the
current policy’s geometry), the term
$`\Delta\theta^{T}\mathbf{F}\Delta\theta`$ grows rapidly, signifying a
departure from the trust region. By enforcing
$`N_{\text{init}}\gg N_{\text{ref}}`$ (small $`\lambda`$), the term
$`(1-\lambda)g_{\text{init}}`$ acts as a regularization term (an
”Anchor”). It ensures that the primary update direction respects the
local curvature $`\mathbf{F}`$, while $`g_{\text{ref}}`$ acts as a small
perturbation vector that rotates the policy toward higher reward regions
without shattering the manifold. ∎

Datasets and Evaluation Metrics. We use randomly sampled subsets of 4k
examples from a reorganized 45k subset ([Yan et al., 2025](#bib.bib42))
of OpenR1-Math-220k ([Bakouch et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)) as the training
set (as described in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Limitations of RL and the Promise of Natural Language Guidance ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")).
For validation, we use the curated validation set provided by ([Yan et
al., 2025](#bib.bib42)). We evaluate the model on five well-established
mathematical reasoning benchmarks: MATH-500 ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib33)), Minerva-Math ([Lewkowycz et al., 2022](#bib.bib34)),
OlympiadBench ([He et al., 2024b](#bib.bib19)), AIME 2024 ([Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib55)), AIME 2025 ([Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib55)), and AMC
2023 ([Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib55)). For broader analysis, we assess
the model’s generalization ability on three scientific and general
reasoning tasks: TheoremQA (Math, Physics, EE&CS, and Finance) ([Chen et
al., 2023](#bib.bib18)), GPQA-Diamond (Physics, Chemistry, and
Biology) ([Rein et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)), and MMLU-Pro (Business,
Computer Science, Law, *etc.*) ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib57)). During
evaluation, we use greedy decoding (temperature = 0) and report pass@1
over three runs.

Reward Design. During RL fine-tuning, we use model-based evaluation to
generate critiques and rule-based evaluation to provide binary scalar
rewards, as described in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Limitations of RL and the Promise of Natural Language Guidance ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").

Compared Methods. We compare Critique-GRPO against the following
representative approaches, categorized into supervised learning and
reinforcement learning-based finetuning. All differences are considered
significant at $`p<0.01`$.

Supervised Learning-based Finetuning:

$`(\textup{i})`$ Supervised Finetuning (SFT): Finetuning the base model
on high-quality annotated training data using supervised learning.

$`(\textup{ii})`$ Reward rAnked Finetuning (RAFT) ([Dong et al.,
2023](#bib.bib50)): Finetuning on self-generated correct responses,
sampled based on rule-based evaluation.

$`(\textup{iii})`$ Refinement Finetuning (Refinement FT) ([Chen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib65)): Finetuning on refined correct responses generated
conditionally on the question, initial response, and CoT critiques.

$`(\textup{iv})`$ Critique Finetuning (Critique FT) ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41)): Finetuning on annotated CoT critique data to train
the model to critique a given query-response.

$`(\textup{v})`$ Critique-in-the-Loop Finetuning (CITL-FT) ([Xi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib44)): Finetuning on mixed data consisting of
self-generated correct responses and refined correct responses,
conditioned on the question-initial response-CoT critique triplet.

Reinforcement Learning-based Finetuning:

$`(\textup{vi})`$ R1-GRPO ([DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)):
Finetuning the base model on its own generations using the GRPO
algorithm with binary scalar rewards.

$`(\textup{vii})`$ R1-Dr.GRPO ([Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib16)):
Finetuning the base model on its own generations using the Dr.GRPO
algorithm, which removes terms that cause biased optimization, with
binary scalar rewards.

$`(\textup{viii})`$ Critique-GRPO (Indicative Critique): Fine-tuning the
base model with Critique-GRPO by utilizing indicative critiques for
refinements, as described in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Limitations of RL with Numerical Feedback and the Promise of Natural Language Guidance (Detailed Analyses) ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").

$`(\textup{ix})`$ Critique-GRPO (Critique with Ground Truth):
Fine-tuning the base model with Critique-GRPO by leveraging indicative
critiques alongside ground-truth answers for refinements, as detailed in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Limitations of RL with Numerical Feedback and the Promise of Natural Language Guidance (Detailed Analyses) ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").

Implementation Details. We conduct experiments using Qwen2.5-7B-Base,
Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Base, and Qwen3-8B, with GPT-4o (which can be replaced
by other reasoning-based reward models) serving as the reward model, as
described in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Limitations of RL and the Promise of Natural Language Guidance ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").
For supervised finetuning baselines, models are finetuned until
convergence, and the best performance is reported. For RL-based
approaches, models are finetuned for 400 steps, and the best performance
is recorded. To ensure a fair comparison: In R1-GRPO, 8 responses
(rollouts) are sampled per training prompt with a temperature of 1. In
Critique-GRPO, 7 responses are sampled per prompt, along with one
refined response from the refinement sets. we present detailed
hyperparameters and training configurations in
Table [13](#A7.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Appendix G Implementation Details ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").

All experiments are conducted on 40 NVIDIA A800 80G GPUs. To ensure
consistency, we use only critiques generated by the reward model that
align with rule-based evaluations; otherwise, the reward model is
prompted to regenerate the critiques. Following prior works ([Liu et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib16)), for evaluation, we adopt greedy sampling
(temperature set to 0) to generate responses and report pass@1 as the
evaluation metric. When reporting pass@k, we uniformly set the
temperature to 0.6 and the top-p value to 0.95.

Compared Methods in the Investigation of Math-Centric Backbone Models.
We evaluate the efficacy of RL fine-tuning with Critique-GRPO on the
math-centric backbone model, Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Base. Specifically, we
compare its performance against three representative RL fine-tuning
approaches based solely on numerical feedback:

$`(\textup{i})`$ SimpleRL-Zero ([Zeng et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)): an
open-source reproduction of R1-GRPO.

$`(\textup{ii})`$ PRIME-Zero ([Cui et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22)):
fine-tuning the base model using both outcome binary rewards and process
binary rewards.

$`(\textup{iii})`$ Oat-Zero ([Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib16)):
fine-tuning the base model with Dr.GRPO using outcome binary rewards.

Figure 9: Comparison of Pass@k for self-improvement using RL fine-tuning

To explore the potential of Critique-GRPO in enabling an LLM’s
self-improvement through self-critiquing, we prompt the model itself to
serve as a reasoning-based reward model. Specifically, we investigate
two types of self-critiquing: $`(\textup{i})`$ Self-critique, where the
model evaluates the correctness of its own responses using CoT critiques
with ground truth answers as reference; and $`(\textup{ii})`$
Self-critique & self-evaluation ([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib59)),
where the model evaluates its responses using CoT critiques without any
reference. These approaches result in Critique-GRPO (self-critique) and
Critique-GRPO (self-critique & self-evaluation), respectively. Details
of the prompts are provided in
Appendix [M](#A13 "Appendix M Prompts ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").

shows the evaluation results on Qwen3-8B, and
Figure [9](#A8.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix H Detailed Results and Analysis of Self-Critiquing Mechanisms ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")
presents pass@k performance changes on AIME24 and AIME25 ([Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib55)).

Critique-GRPO enhances self-improvement through self-critiquing.
Table [14](#A8.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix H Detailed Results and Analysis of Self-Critiquing Mechanisms ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")
RL fine-tuning with Critique-GRPO (self-critique) significantly
outperforms fine-tuning with GRPO using external numerical feedback
(R1-GRPO) and supervised fine-tuning with expert demonstrations (SFT).
On average, Critique-GRPO (self-critique) improves pass@1 by +4.5% and
+12.0% compared to R1-GRPO and SFT, respectively. Additionally, the
unsupervised approach—Critique-GRPO (self-critique &
self-evaluation)—achieves an average pass@1 improvement of 2.3% over
R1-GRPO, highlighting the potential of leveraging self-critique for
self-improvement without any external supervision.

Self-critiquing aids effective exploration.
Figure [9](#A8.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix H Detailed Results and Analysis of Self-Critiquing Mechanisms ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")
highlights the consistently superior performance of Critique-GRPO
(self-critique) across pass@k metrics, with $`k`$ ranging from 1 to 256,
indicating genuine improvements. Notably, Critique-GRPO (self-critique)
achieves remarkable gains over R1-GRPO for pass@k with $`k=1`$ to $`4`$,
yielding improvements of 10-16.7% on AIME24
(Figure [9(a)](#A8.F9.sf1 "Figure 9(a) ‣ Figure 9 ‣ Appendix H Detailed Results and Analysis of Self-Critiquing Mechanisms ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")).

## Appendix I Detailed Investigation of Policy Exploration During RL Finetuning

![Refer to caption](2506.03106v7/floats/raw_figures/entropy_qwen25.png)

(a) Entropy dynamics for RL-based finetuning approaches over training
steps on Qwen2.5-7B-Base.

![Refer to
caption](2506.03106v7/floats/raw_figures/self_critique_cross_entropy_qwen3.png)

(b) Entropy dynamics of self-improvement through self-critiquing and
weak-to-strong generalization across training steps on Qwen3-8B.

Figure 10: Entropy dynamics during RL finetuning. A comparison of
RL-based finetuning approaches for self-improvement on Qwen2.5-7B-Base
(left) and self-improvement through self-critiquing with Critique-GRPO
on Qwen3-8B (right).

To investigate policy exploration, we analyze two primary aspects of our
RL-finetuned models: $`(\textup{i})`$ entropy dynamics during RL
fine-tuning for self-improvement using compared RL-based finetuning
approaches on Qwen2.5-7B-Base and Critique-GRPO (self-critique) on
Qwen3-8B
(Figure [10](#A9.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Appendix I Detailed Investigation of Policy Exploration During RL Finetuning ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")),
and $`(\textup{ii})`$ changes in response length during fine-tuning
(Figure [11](#A9.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Appendix I Detailed Investigation of Policy Exploration During RL Finetuning ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")).

Learning from natural language feedback helps sustain exploration. As
shown in
Figure [10(a)](#A9.F10.sf1 "Figure 10(a) ‣ Figure 10 ‣ Appendix I Detailed Investigation of Policy Exploration During RL Finetuning ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
the policy entropy of Critique-GRPO generally remains higher than that
of R1-GRPO and R1-Dr.GRPO, suggesting more consistent exploration. The
peaks in Critique-GRPO’s entropy dynamics (before step 200) likely occur
when its self-generated refinements deviate significantly from the
initial sampled responses, leading to increased entropy and potentially
beneficial distributional shifts. The subsequent decrease in entropy
indicates that the model quickly internalizes these refinements,
reducing the distributional deviation. This dynamic aligns with the
observation that rare actions with high advantage can increase policy
entropy (*i.e.,* unfamiliar but correct responses with high rewards
promote effective exploration), whereas high-probability actions with
high advantage tend to reduce entropy ([Cui et al., 2025b](#bib.bib51)).
In contrast, R1-GRPO exhibits entropy collapse, where policy entropy
drops sharply at the start of training and continues to decline
monotonically to near zero. R1-Dr.GRPO initially exhibits higher entropy
(before step 50) but rapidly drops to comparable near-zero values with
R1-GRPO after step 150. Combined with the results in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
the superior performance of Critique-GRPO over R1-Dr.GRPO and R1-GRPO
highlights the importance of maintaining a certain level of entropy for
better performance.

Learning through self-critiquing facilitates policy exploration.
Figure [10(b)](#A9.F10.sf2 "Figure 10(b) ‣ Figure 10 ‣ Appendix I Detailed Investigation of Policy Exploration During RL Finetuning ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")
shows that Critique-GRPO (self-critique) avoids entropy collapse and
maintains higher entropy than R1-GRPO. This finding aligns with the
observation that increased exploration improves performance.

![Refer to
caption](2506.03106v7/floats/raw_figures/response_length_qwen25.png)

(a) Response length changes on Qwen2.5-7B-Base.

![Refer to caption](2506.03106v7/floats/raw_figures/qwen3_length.png)

(b) Response length changes on Qwen3-8B.

Figure 11: Comparison of response length changes during RL finetuning on
Qwen2.5-7B-Base (left) and Qwen3-8B (right).

Higher entropy does not always guarantee effective exploration.
Unexpectedly, as shown in
Figure [10(b)](#A9.F10.sf2 "Figure 10(b) ‣ Figure 10 ‣ Appendix I Detailed Investigation of Policy Exploration During RL Finetuning ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
Critique-GRPO (weaker refinement via critique with ground truth), shown
in green, achieves higher entropy than Critique-GRPO (self-critique),
shown in dark blue, yet performs worse (average pass@1: 65.55% v.s.
68.13%). This discrepancy may be due to refinements from weaker models
causing larger distributional shifts compared to self-refinements, while
also being of lower quality. This suggests that the quality of
exploration signals is more critical than the extent of exploration (as
reflected solely by entropy).

Critique-GRPO facilitates concise reasoning. In
Figure [11](#A9.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Appendix I Detailed Investigation of Policy Exploration During RL Finetuning ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"),
Critique-GRPO achieves superior performance
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback"))
while minimally increasing response length on Qwen2.5-7B-Base
(Figure [11(a)](#A9.F11.sf1 "Figure 11(a) ‣ Figure 11 ‣ Appendix I Detailed Investigation of Policy Exploration During RL Finetuning ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")).
This efficiency likely stems from its critique mechanism, which enables
precise error identification and refinement, reducing the need for
verbose reasoning. Additionally, Critique-GRPO tends to reduce response
length on Qwen3-8B
(Figure [11(b)](#A9.F11.sf2 "Figure 11(b) ‣ Figure 11 ‣ Appendix I Detailed Investigation of Policy Exploration During RL Finetuning ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")).
This trend can be attributed to the correction of Qwen3-8B’s tendency
toward redundant and ineffective self-reflection, as discussed in
Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Qualitative Analysis ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").

## Appendix J Qualitative Analysis

Fine-Grained Analysis. We conduct a fine-grained analysis of 100
generated responses on the Minerva-MATH dataset across four key
dimensions: factuality, conciseness, correctness, and logicality, using
the prompt in
Appendix [M](#A13 "Appendix M Prompts ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").
Figure [12](#A10.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ Appendix J Qualitative Analysis ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")
shows that fine-tuning with Critique-GRPO on Qwen2.5-7B-Base achieves
the best performance across all four dimensions as well as in average
performance. Additionally, the superior performance of RL fine-tuning
with Critique-GRPO over R1-GRPO in terms of factuality and correctness
indicates that CoT critiques help the model effectively identify errors
and improve valid exploration. The inferior performance of SFT in
logicality and conciseness may be attributed to the presence of
redundant and sometimes illogical self-reflective reasoning behaviors in
expert demonstrations, which could negatively impact user experience.

![Refer to
caption](2506.03106v7/floats/raw_figures/fine_grained_evaluation.png)

Figure 12: Qualitative analysis of generated responses on Minerva-Math
across four dimensions: logicality, factuality, conciseness,
correctness, and average performance.

Case Study. We present a qualitative comparison between the responses
generated by the base Qwen3-8B model and the RL-finetuned Qwen3-8B model
using Critique-GRPO on the MATH-500 dataset. The given question is:
Evaluate
$`\sin(\arcsin 0.4+\arcsin 0.5),\sin(\arcsin 0.5-\arcsin 0.4)`$.

The base Qwen3-8B model produces an incorrect response due to an
incorrect formulation of the expression as
$`\sin(A+B)\cdot{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\sin(A-B)}`$, as shown in the red
square. In contrast, the RL-finetuned Qwen3-8B model using Critique-GRPO
generates a correct response by correctly formulating the expression as
$`\sin(\alpha+\beta)\cdot{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\sin(\beta-\alpha)}`$, as
shown in the green square. Furthermore, the base Qwen3-8B model exhibits
numerous redundant and ineffective self-reflection attempts (*e.g.,*
“Wait, …” highlighted in blue), which fail to help the model identify
the actual errors and answer the question correctly. This results in an
excessively long response (over 6000 tokens). In contrast, the
RL-finetuned Qwen3-8B model using Critique-GRPO demonstrates concise and
effective reasoning. It remains on the correct path to solve the
problem, exhibits valid self-reflection to validate the answer (*e.g.,*
“Let me check with approximate values. …”), and ultimately generates the
correct answer. Detailed responses are provided in
Appendix [O](#A15 "Appendix O Responses Utilized in Qualitative Analysis ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").

## Appendix K Limitations

While Critique-GRPO establishes a promising foundation for leveraging
both natural language and numerical feedback, notable limitations
remain.

Performance limitations due to failed refinements. Policy models
sometimes fail to follow CoT critiques to refine their responses. We
attribute this to the lack of deliberate training for self-refinement.
An example of a failed refinement is provided in
Appendix [P](#A16 "Appendix P An Example of Failed Refinement ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback").
Future work could focus on improving the model’s refinement capabilities
or training a specialized model dedicated to refinement tasks.

The role of critique detail in refinement quality. We currently utilize
three types of critiques (see
Section [3](#S3 "3 Limitations of RL and the Promise of Natural Language Guidance ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")),
with CoT critiques demonstrating the greatest benefits for refinement.
This advantage likely stems from their detailed step-by-step evaluations
and concise improvement suggestions, which help models identify and
correct errors in initial responses. It follows that more detailed
critiques could result in higher-quality refinements. For simplicity, we
use GPT-4o as the reasoning-based reward model, not for expert knowledge
distillation. Consequently, the generated CoT critiques do not include
expert demonstrations. Future work may explore alternative
reasoning-based reward models. One might assume that directly
incorporating expert demonstrations into critiques would significantly
improve performance. However, our experiments reveal otherwise. Upon
analyzing the generated refinements, we observe that both pre-trained
models (*e.g.,* Qwen2.5-7B-Base) and alignment-tuned models (*e.g.,*
Qwen3-8B) tend to produce conclusive sentences and correct answers as
refinements, rather than detailed step-by-step reasoning to derive the
correct answer. This behavior limits the effectiveness of expert
demonstrations as critiques.

Future work could investigate, in greater depth, which types of
critiques provide the most significant benefits for refinement,
particularly in reasoning-intensive tasks.

## Appendix L Analysis of Cognitive Behaviors

To systematically investigate this question, we characterize six key
cognitive behaviors that contribute to self-improving reasoning during
RL fine-tuning, as follows:

- •
  Subgoal Setting: Breaking down complex problems into smaller,
  manageable steps or subtasks. For example, “Step 1… Step 2…”
- •
  Summarization: Summarizing the current state by identifying completed
  subtasks and determining what remains to be done. This helps guide the
  next steps in reasoning. For example, “Now we have obtained…, next, we
  need to…”
- •
  Verification: Systematically checking intermediate results or
  computations to ensure correctness. For example, “Let’s verify this
  result by…”
- •
  Backtracking: Identifying errors or dead-ends in reasoning and
  explicitly revising previous methods or approaches. For example, “This
  approach won’t work because…, let’s try another method…”
- •
  Backward Chaining: Reasoning from desired outcomes back to initial
  inputs or steps required to achieve the result. This is particularly
  applicable to multiple-choice questions where answer options are
  provided. For example, “To get 24, I could do 24 ÷ 2 = 12…” ([Gandhi
  et al., 2025](#bib.bib17))
- •
  Anticipation: Anticipating potential inaccuracies or exhaustively
  considering multiple possibilities to solve a problem. For example,
  “Alternatively, this problem can be solved by…”

We analyze the reasoning (cognitive) behaviors using the prompts shown
below.

When assessing the contributions of reasoning behaviors in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Limitations of RL and the Promise of Natural Language Guidance ‣ Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback")
to successful problem-solving in RL fine-tuned models, we count each
behavior appearing in the generated responses only once. For example, if
the model produces multiple subgoals in a single response, the
occurrence of “subgoal setting” is counted as one.

##### Prompt for Generating Chain-of-Thought Critique.

We adopt a prompt inspired by ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)) to
enable GPT-4o ([Hurst et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)) to generate CoT
critiques. For quality control, we retained only those model-generated
critiques whose evaluative conclusions (correct/incorrect) aligned with
rule-based verification. When inconsistencies occurred, we prompted the
critique model to regenerate the critiques.
````
